newsitem.title: FINLAND: Neste to cut back oil trading ops - COO.
newsitem.headline: Neste to cut back oil trading ops - COO.

text.p: Finnish oil and energy group Neste Oy will cut back its oil trading operations after heavy trading losses in 1996, but will not withdraw entirely from trading, Neste's chief operating officer said on Friday.

"From our point of view it would make sense (for trading) to go below 10 billion markka ($2 billion) in net sales," group president and COO Jukka Viinanen told a news conference after Neste reported 1996 profits down 59 percent on 1995.

Group profit before extraordinary items and taxes fell to 566 million markka from 1.36 billion in 1996, mainly due to 560 million markka losses in oil trading and to weak profits at its half-owned Borealis petrochemicals unit, Neste said.

In 1996, oil trading accounted for about 16 billion markka of Neste's 43.4 billion markka net sales, Viinanen said, adding that the trading operations' slice of net sales was down from about 19 billion markka in 1995 and would continue to decline.

The full-year 1996 trading losses exceeded the 495 million markka loss stated in Neste's eight-month report in October due to the stronger dollar and to charges against the 1996 result of commitments falling due in the last quarter of 1997, Neste said.
But the company said it no longer had major exposure to trading losses, and that it would continue to trade.
"It is not possible to withdraw entirely from trading," Viinanen said. "We need to be in touch with the market."
Neste has fully revised its trading rules, risk limits and system of control, Viinanen said.
"We intend to live with these rules and review the situation again at the end of the year," he said.

Viinanen declined to comment on crude oil price trends this year, but said that the refining margin -- now at about $1-1.50 per barrel -- was unsatisfactory and was expected to remain at that level this year.

That level would not permit further investment in oil refining and, in the longer term, investment in refining in Europe would only become possible if the refining margin returned to about $2.50-$4 per barrel, he said.
